title: Master Table of Standard Derivatives & Differentiation Rules
answer: Standard derivatives in differential calculus include: d/dx(xⁿ) = n·xⁿ⁻¹, d/dx(eˣ) = eˣ, d/dx(ln x) = 1/x, d/dx(sin x) = cos x, d/dx(cos x) = -sin x, d/dx(tan x) = sec²x, d/dx(arcsin x) = 1/√(1 - x²), and d/dx(arctan x) = 1/(1 + x²).
highlights: Trigonometric Derivatives: d/dx(sin x) = cos x; d/dx(cos x) = -sin x; d/dx(tan x) = sec²x; d/dx(sec x) = sec x·tan x; d/dx(cot x) = -csc²x; d/dx(csc x) = -csc x·cot x
Inverse Trigonometric: d/dx(arcsin x) = 1/√(1 - x²); d/dx(arccos x) = -1/√(1 - x²); d/dx(arctan x) = 1/(1 + x²); d/dx(arccot x) = -1/(1 + x²)
Exponential & Logarithmic: d/dx(eˣ) = eˣ; d/dx(aˣ) = aˣ·ln(a); d/dx(ln x) = 1/x; d/dx(log_a x) = 1/(x·ln a)
Core Operational Rules: Product Rule (uv)' = u'v + uv'; Quotient Rule (u/v)' = (u'v - uv')/v²; Chain Rule d/dx[f(g(x))] = f'(g(x))·g'(x)

title: Master Table of Standard Integrals & Integration by Parts
answer: Integration by Parts is given by: ∫ u dv = u·v - ∫ v du (following the ILATE priority rule: Inverse trig, Logarithmic, Algebraic, Trigonometric, Exponential). Standard indefinite integrals include: ∫ (1 / (a² + x²)) dx = (1/a)·arctan(x/a) + C, and ∫ (1 / √(a² - x²)) dx = arcsin(x/a) + C.
highlights: Integration by Parts: ∫ u·(dv/dx) dx = u·v - ∫ v·(du/dx) dx (ILATE priority for choosing u)
Trigonometric Integrals: ∫ tan x dx = ln|sec x| + C; ∫ cot x dx = ln|sin x| + C; ∫ sec x dx = ln|sec x + tan x| + C; ∫ csc x dx = ln|csc x - cot x| + C

Special Algebraic Integrals: ∫ 1/(a² + x²) dx = (1/a)·arctan(x/a) + C; ∫ 1/√(a² - x²) dx = arcsin(x/a) + C; ∫ 1/√(x² ± a²) dx = ln|x + √(x² ± a²)| + C; ∫ 1/(x² - a²) dx = (1/2a)·ln|(x - a)/(x + a)| + C
Fundamental Theorem of Calculus: If F'(x) = f(x), then ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = F(b) - F(a)

keywords: mean median mode variance standard deviation
title: Statistics: Central Tendency, Standard Deviation & Normal Distribution
answer: In statistics, the empirical relationship between measures of central tendency for moderately skewed distributions is: Mode = 3·Median - 2·Mean. Standard Deviation measures dispersion: σ = √[(Σ (x - μ)²) / N]. For a normal distribution, the 68–95–99.7 rule states that 68.27% of data lies within μ ± 1σ, 95.45% within μ ± 2σ, and 99.73% within μ ± 3σ.
highlights: Empirical Central Tendency Formula: Mode = 3·Median - 2·Mean
Variance & Standard Deviation: Variance σ² = [Σ(x_i - μ)²] / N; Standard Deviation σ = √(Variance)
Coefficient of Variation (CV): CV = (σ / Mean) × 100% (measures relative dispersion/consistency)
Normal Distribution (68–95–99.7 Empirical Rule): 68.27% within ±1σ, 95.45% within ±2σ, 99.73% within ±3σ around mean μ

title: Number Theory: Euclidean Algorithm & Fermat's Little Theorem
answer: The Euclidean Algorithm computes the Greatest Common Divisor (GCD / HCF) of two integers by repeated division: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b) until remainder is zero. Fermat's Little Theorem states that if p is a prime number and a is an integer not divisible by p, then a^(p-1) ≡ 1 (mod p) [or a^p ≡ a (mod p)].
highlights: Euclidean Algorithm: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b) (Extremely efficient, logarithmic time complexity O(log(min(a, b))))
Bézout's Identity: For any integers a and b, there exist integers x and y such that ax + by = gcd(a, b)
Fermat's Little Theorem: a^(p-1) ≡ 1 (mod p) for prime p and gcd(a, p) = 1 (Foundation of RSA public-key cryptography and primality tests)
Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic: Every integer n > 1 can be uniquely represented as a product of prime powers up to the order of factors

title: Coordinate Geometry & Conic Sections (Line, Circle, Parabola, Ellipse, Hyperbola)
answer: Conic sections are curves obtained by intersecting a plane with a double right circular cone, classified by eccentricity e: Circle (e = 0), Parabola (e = 1: y² = 4ax), Ellipse (0 < e < 1: x²/a² + y²/b² = 1 where b² = a²(1 - e²)), and Hyperbola (e > 1: x²/a² - y²/b² = 1 where b² = a²(e² - 1)).
highlights: Perpendicular Distance of Point (x₀, y₀) from Line Ax + By + C = 0: d = |Ax₀ + By₀ + C| / √(A² + B²)
Circle: (x - h)² + (y - k)² = r² (Center (h, k), Radius r)
Parabola: y² = 4ax (Eccentricity e = 1, Focus (a, 0), Directrix x = -a, Length of Latus Rectum = 4a)
Ellipse: x²/a² + y²/b² = 1 (0 < e < 1, Foci (±ae, 0), Directrices x = ±a/e, Latus Rectum = 2b²/a)
Hyperbola: x²/a² - y²/b² = 1 (e > 1, Foci (±ae, 0), Directrices x = ±a/e, Asymptotes y = ±(b/a)x)

title: Vector Algebra & 3D Geometry Formulas
answer: The Dot Product of two vectors is a scalar a · b = |a||b|cos θ = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + a₃b₃ (zero when orthogonal). The Cross Product is a vector a × b = |a||b|sin θ n̂ (magnitude equals the area of a parallelogram). The Scalar Triple Product [a b c] = a · (b × c) equals the volume of the parallelepiped formed by the three vectors.
highlights: Dot Product: a · b = |a||b|cos(θ); Condition for Perpendicularity: a · b = 0
Cross Product: a × b = det([i, j, k], [a₁, a₂, a₃], [b₁, b₂, b₃]); Area of triangle = ½|a × b|
Scalar Triple Product: [a b c] = det([a₁, a₂, a₃], [b₁, b₂, b₃], [c₁, c₂, c₃]); Condition for Coplanarity: [a b c] = 0
3D Line Equation: (x - x₁)/a = (y - y₁)/b = (z - z₁)/c; 3D Plane Equation: A(x - x₁) + B(y - y₁) + C(z - z₁) = 0

title: Complex Numbers, De Moivre's Theorem & Cube Roots of Unity
answer: A complex number is represented in polar form as z = a + ib = r(cos θ + i sin θ) = re^(iθ), with modulus r = √(a² + b²) and argument θ = arctan(b/a). De Moivre's Theorem states that (cos θ + i sin θ)ⁿ = cos(nθ) + i sin(nθ). The three cube roots of unity are 1, ω = (-1 + i√3)/2, and ω² = (-1 - i√3)/2, satisfying 1 + ω + ω² = 0 and ω³ = 1.
highlights: De Moivre's Theorem: [r(cos θ + i sin θ)]ⁿ = rⁿ(cos nθ + i sin nθ) = rⁿ e^(inθ)
Cube Roots of Unity: Roots of x³ - 1 = 0 are 1, ω, ω² where ω = e^(i2π/3) = -½ + i(√3/2)
Key Identities of Unity Roots: 1 + ω + ω² = 0, ω³ = 1, ω^(3k) = 1, ω^(3k+1) = ω, ω^(3k+2) = ω²
Conjugate Properties: |z| = |z̄|; z · z̄ = |z|²; (z₁ + z₂)̄ = z̄₁ + z̄₂; (z₁z₂)̄ = z̄₁z̄₂

keywords: greens theorem stokes theorem divergence theorem
title: Fundamental Theorems of Vector Calculus
answer: Vector calculus unites field integrals: (1) Green's Theorem: ∮ (L dx + M dy) = ∬ (∂M/∂x - ∂L/∂y) dA, (2) Stokes' Theorem: ∮ F · dr = ∬ (∇ × F) · dS (relates line integral around boundary to surface integral of curl), (3) Divergence Theorem (Gauss): ∬ F · dS = ∭ (∇ · F) dV (relates flux through closed surface to volume integral of divergence).
highlights: Gradient (∇f): Vector of partial derivatives pointing in direction of maximum rate of increase
Divergence (∇ · F): Scalar measure of field source/sink density (zero for incompressible/solenoidal fields)
Curl (∇ × F): Vector measure of field rotation (zero for conservative/irrotational fields where F = ∇f)
Forms mathematical backbone of Maxwell's equations and fluid mechanics (Navier-Stokes)

title: Fourier Series and Continuous Fourier Transform
answer: Fourier Series decomposes any periodic function f(t) of period T into an infinite sum of sines and cosines: f(t) = a₀/2 + Σ [a_n cos(nω₀t) + b_n sin(nω₀t)]. The continuous Fourier Transform converts non-periodic signals from time to frequency domain: F(ω) = ∫ f(t) e^(-iωt) dt. Fast Fourier Transform (FFT, Cooley-Tukey) computes Discrete FT in O(N log N) instead of O(N²).
highlights: Orthogonality of sinusoidal basis functions enables exact coefficient extraction
Inverse Fourier Transform: f(t) = (1/2π) ∫ F(ω) e^(iωt) dω
Parseval's Theorem: Total energy in time domain equals total energy in frequency domain: ∫ |f(t)|² dt = (1/2π) ∫ |F(ω)|² dω
Ubiquitous in signal processing, image compression (JPEG DCT), quantum wave mechanics, and audio synthesis

keywords: characteristic equation det A - lambda I = 0
title: Eigenvalues, Eigenvectors, and Matrix Diagonalization
answer: For a square matrix A, a non-zero vector v is an eigenvector and λ is its corresponding eigenvalue if Av = λv. Eigenvalues are the roots of the characteristic polynomial det(A - λI) = 0. A matrix is diagonalizable as A = PDP⁻¹ where D is the diagonal matrix of eigenvalues and P is the matrix of eigenvectors.
highlights: Trace of A equals sum of all eigenvalues: Tr(A) = Σ λ_i
Determinant of A equals product of all eigenvalues: det(A) = Π λ_i
Symmetric real matrices (A = Aᵀ) always have real eigenvalues and orthogonal eigenvectors (Spectral Theorem)
Foundational in Principal Component Analysis (PCA), Google PageRank, Quantum state operators, and vibration modes

title: Standard Algebraic Identities & Factorization Formulas
answer: Essential algebraic identities: (1) (a+b)² = a² + 2ab + b², (2) (a-b)² = a² - 2ab + b², (3) a² - b² = (a-b)(a+b), (4) (a+b)³ = a³ + 3a²b + 3ab² + b³ = a³ + b³ + 3ab(a+b), (5) a³ + b³ = (a+b)(a² - ab + b²), (6) a³ - b³ = (a-b)(a² + ab + b²), (7) a³ + b³ + c³ - 3abc = (a+b+c)(a² + b² + c² - ab - bc - ca).
highlights: (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b²
(a - b)² = a² - 2ab + b²
a² - b² = (a - b)(a + b)
(a + b + c)² = a² + b² + c² + 2(ab + bc + ca)
a³ + b³ = (a + b)(a² - ab + b²)
a³ - b³ = (a - b)(a² + ab + b²)
Special condition: If a + b + c = 0, then a³ + b³ + c³ = 3abc

answer: Key 3D solid formulas: Cube (V = a³, TSA = 6a²), Cuboid (V = lbh, TSA = 2(lb+bh+hl)), Cylinder (V = πr²h, CSA = 2πrh, TSA = 2πr(r+h)), Cone (V = ⅓πr²h, CSA = πrl where l=√(r²+h²), TSA = πr(r+l)), Sphere (V = ⁴⁄₃πr³, TSA = 4πr²), Hemisphere (V = ⅔πr³, CSA = 2πr², TSA = 3πr²).
highlights: Sphere (radius r): Volume = (4/3)πr³ | Surface Area = 4πr²
Hemisphere: Volume = (2/3)πr³ | Curved Surface = 2πr² | Total Surface Area = 3πr²
Cylinder (radius r, height h): Volume = πr²h | CSA = 2πrh | TSA = 2πr(r + h)

title: Conic Sections — Circle, Parabola, Ellipse, Hyperbola

highlights: Circle (center (h,k), radius r): (x - h)² + (y - k)² = r² | Eccentricity e = 0

Hyperbola (transverse axis 2a, conjugate 2b): x²/a² - y²/b² = 1 | Foci (±ae, 0) | e = √(1 + b²/a²) > 1
Asymptotes of hyperbola: y = ±(b/a)x
